name: Doublecheck (working name) — the write-action reconciliation layer for AI agents
one_liner: For engineering teams running production AI agents that touch money, tickets and customer comms, Doublecheck is a thin proxy + console that records every external write an agent attempts, resolves "did this actually commit?" when a tool call times out, and blocks duplicate payments, emails and refunds on retry or fork.
problem: Teams shipping agents that perform real write actions (charge a card, issue a refund, send a customer email, create a Jira/Zendesk ticket, update a CRM record) hit a specific failure that generic observability does not solve: a tool call times out or the process dies after the external system already committed the action. On retry, resume or fork, the agent redoes it — duplicate refund, duplicate invoice, the same apology email twice, three tickets for one complaint. @paddix (DigitalOcean) names this precisely: "If a tool times out after submitting a payment, blindly replaying the step can duplicate the payment… You need recorded step outcomes, idempotency where supported, and reconciliation when the result is uncertain." Today teams handle this by hand: engineers write per-integration idempotency keys (only some APIs support them), wrap steps in Temporal/Inngest activities, and when something looks wrong an on-call engineer opens Stripe, the mail provider and the CRM in three tabs and manually checks whether the action landed. That fails because (a) durable execution guarantees the workflow replays, not that the external world only changed once — the engine has no idea what the third-party API did during the timeout window; (b) tracing tools (LangSmith, Langfuse, Braintrust) record that a call was made and what it cost, not whether its effect exists in the target system; (c) nobody has a per-tenant ledger that answers "what did this agent actually change out there in the last hour, and is any of it duplicated?"
target_customer: Buyer: the engineering lead / platform owner (Head of AI Engineering, Staff Eng on the agent platform team) at a 30–500 person company that has moved an agent from demo to production on write paths. Concretely: fintech and vertical-SaaS teams whose agents do billing ops, refunds, collections, claims, order changes, or outbound customer email at volume. Secondary buyer in regulated shops: the risk/compliance owner who needs an action-level audit trail. Not a fit: chat-only or read-only RAG assistants — no side effects, no pain.
why_now: Three things converged in 2026. First, agents moved from read to write: the bookmarked DigitalOcean thread, and the Jaya Gupta/Ashu Garg piece it responds to, argue the expanding "execution workload around inference" is now the architectural unit of the AI cloud — i.e. actions, not tokens. Second, durable execution became default plumbing (Temporal, Restate, Inngest, DBOS, LangGraph checkpoints are now standard in agent stacks per multiple 2026 comparisons), which makes replay-after-crash routine and therefore makes duplicate-side-effect risk routine. Third, tool fan-out exploded: gateways and marketplaces like Monid (1,700+ tools, 55+ providers behind one connection) and Vercel AI Gateway tool providers mean an agent can call dozens of third-party write APIs the team never individually hardened for idempotency. The number of "uncertain outcome" moments per company per week is rising fast; nobody owns resolving them.
comparables:
Durable execution engines — Temporal, Restate, Inngest, DBOS, Hatchet, Trigger.dev (see 2026 priced comparison at startupik.com and ZenML's Temporal-alternatives roundup). They give exactly-once *workflow step recording* and retries; they explicitly do not verify what a third-party API did during a timeout, and they require you to restructure code into workflows. Gap: outcome resolution against the external system, and adoption without rewriting the agent.
LLM/agent observability — LangSmith, Langfuse (open source), Braintrust, Helicone, Arize Phoenix, Pydantic Logfire. These trace calls, cost, latency and evals. They are read-only on the world: none of them will tell you "this refund exists twice in Stripe." Gap: write-action semantics and blocking.
MCP/AI gateways — TrueFoundry, Kong AI Gateway, LiteLLM, Cequence, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. These sit in the right place in the stack (policy, credentials, allow/deny per tool) and are the most likely to absorb this feature. Today their framing is security/governance and token cost, not duplicate-effect prevention or reconciliation. Gap: the dedup ledger and the "uncertain outcome" queue.
FinOps-for-AI — Revenium, Mavvrik, nOps, PointFive, plus the FinOps Foundation's token-economics working group, all converging on "cost per successful task." They count dollars spent on inference; they do not count dollars wrongly moved by duplicate actions. Different problem, adjacent buyer.
Honest uncertainty: I did not find a named, funded company selling write-action reconciliation for agents as its core product. That could mean the gap is real, or that it is being quietly shipped inside the gateways above. Treat the "no direct competitor" claim as unverified, not proven.
market_note: Estimates, clearly labelled. Pricing anchor from the category: agent observability sells at roughly $50–$500/month entry and lands in the low tens of thousands ARR for serious teams; durable-execution cloud lands similarly. Doublecheck should price on write actions, not tokens — e.g. $0.002–$0.01 per recorded write action with a $500–$2,000/month floor, because the thing it protects (a duplicated refund, a double charge) is denominated in dollars, which makes ROI arithmetic trivial: one prevented duplicate $400 refund per month pays for a starter plan. Plausible initial buyer universe is narrow — my estimate is low thousands of companies worldwide in 2026 have agents making real-money writes at volume — so this is a $5–15M ARR wedge in the near term, expanding as write-agents spread. Willingness to pay is highest in fintech/payments and insurance claims, where a duplicate action is a chargeback, a regulatory note, or a customer refund, not just an embarrassment. None of these numbers are sourced figures; they are my estimates from observed category pricing.
risks:
1. Feature absorption. An MCP/AI gateway (TrueFoundry, Kong, LiteLLM, Bedrock AgentCore) or a durable-execution vendor (Temporal, Restate, Inngest) is one quarter away from shipping "idempotent tool calls + effect ledger" as a checkbox. They already sit in the request path and own the policy surface. Doublecheck only survives if the reconciliation connectors — the part that actually queries Stripe/SendGrid/Zendesk to confirm reality — are deep and numerous enough to be a moat.
2. Integration treadmill. The value is per-connector, and correctness depends on each third-party API's quirks (which support idempotency keys, which expose searchable recent-writes, which are eventually consistent). Coverage grows linearly with headcount; that is a bad shape for a small team unless the first version is deliberately limited to 3–5 money-and-comms APIs.
3. Trust and placement. Sitting in the path of payment and customer-email calls means security review, SOC 2 pressure and latency scrutiny from day one — expensive for a seed-stage team. The mitigation (SDK-side, send only hashes and metadata) weakens the blocking capability that makes the product valuable.
riskiest_assumptions:
1. That teams experience duplicate/uncertain write actions often enough to buy a product for it, rather than once a quarter at a scale where a manual check suffices. This is the one to kill first — if the typical team sees two ambiguous writes a month, this is a feature, not a company.
2. That reconciliation can be done usefully with shallow, per-connector probes (search Stripe for a refund with this idempotency key/amount/customer in the last 10 minutes; search the mail provider's sent log for this message-id) rather than needing deep per-API semantics that make every new integration a multi-week build. If each connector is bespoke and brittle, the product never reaches coverage.
3. That teams will route write calls through a third-party proxy holding, or at least seeing, payment and customer-comms traffic. Security review is the likely deal-killer; an in-process SDK that calls out only for the ledger may be the required form factor.
first_customers: Target ten specific, findable teams rather than a persona. (a) YC W26/S26 companies whose one-liner is "AI agent for billing ops / collections / claims / refunds" — filter the YC directory by those keywords and email the technical co-founder; they have write agents and no platform team to build this. (b) Engineers who publicly posted 2026 postmortems or forum threads about agents double-executing side effects — e.g. the authors and commenters on the r/softwarearchitecture durable-execution thread, the "AI Agent Control Flow Patterns" write-up that lists double-executed side effects as a top failure, and Temporal/Restate/Inngest community Slack and Discord channels where "how do I make this tool call idempotent" is asked weekly. (c) Vertical SaaS with agentic refund/claim features — ecommerce support automation and insurtech. Opening ask is not a sale: "send me a redacted trace of your last ambiguous write; I'll tell you within a day whether it duplicated."
validation_test: This week: build the console mock (the prototype below) and run 10 structured 30-minute calls with engineers from the three sources above. Script: "Walk me through the last time an agent of yours wrote to an external system and you weren't sure whether it landed. What did you do? How long did it take? Did it ever duplicate?" PASS if ≥6 of 10 can name a specific incident from the last 90 days, AND ≥4 say an engineer manually checked a third-party console to resolve it, AND ≥3 agree to send a redacted trace or join a design partner call. FAIL if the dominant answer is "our durable execution setup / idempotency keys already handle it" or "it's happened once, we ate it" — in which case reshape toward the compliance/audit-trail framing for regulated buyers, or drop it.
reasoning: Four other candidates lost on gap or buyer. The decisive point for this one: the bookmark that inspired it is not a product launch, it is a practitioner at a cloud provider describing, in operational detail, a failure mode his platform has to handle — recorded step outcomes, idempotency where supported, reconciliation when the result is uncertain. That is a spec for a product nobody in my searches is selling directly. Searches returned dense coverage of the two adjacent categories (durable execution; LLM observability) and confirmed each stops short: durable execution guarantees replay of *your* workflow, observability records *that* a call happened. Neither answers "does the effect exist in the external system, and does it exist twice?" The failure reason I can most plausibly route around is integration treadmill: a first version covering Stripe refunds/charges, one transactional email provider and one ticketing system would already cover the writes that cost actual money, and the "uncertain outcome queue" UI is valuable even when resolution is semi-manual. The post's engagement is low (21 likes) — that is not evidence either way, and I am leaning on the specificity of the failure description, not on the audience's reaction to it.
candidates_considered:
1. Doublecheck — write-action reconciliation and duplicate-effect prevention for production agents (from @paddix). WON: concrete, dollar-denominated pain; adjacent categories demonstrably stop short; narrow first version is shippable.
2. Agent tool-spend FinOps — per-tool, per-customer cost attribution across gateways like Monid and Vercel AI Gateway (from @shengkunye, @vercel_dev). LOST: crowded and well-funded. Revenium, Mavvrik, nOps, PointFive, Zylo plus every observability vendor already ship token and tool cost attribution, and the FinOps Foundation has a working group on it. Gap closed for the same buyer.
3. Spec-to-statechart verification as a service for AI-written code (from @poteto). LOST: the thing described is already a free Cursor plugin skill (pstack) with the /create-formal-verification-skill flow in its public docs; proposing a product here would be cloning a named thing, and formal methods has a thirty-year record of narrow commercial appetite.
4. Agent tool-reliability ratings — an independent uptime/accuracy/cost benchmark for the 1,800+ tools agents call, sitting above Monid-style usage leaderboards. LOST: Monid's own rankings page already occupies the surface and is explicitly usage-based; an independent benchmark is a media property with unclear buyer and no budget owner. Interesting, not investable tonight.
5. Structured-data-for-agents verticalised beyond Tako's finance/sports/weather coverage, e.g. licensed logistics or healthcare pricing data as an agent tool. LOST: the hard part is data licensing, not software; wrong shape for a small technical team and I could not size the rights cost with the tools available.
Skipped as noise: @davidsenra (DHH quote), @nateherk (/roast-room prompt pack), @tsukiema_ (second-brain prompt setup), @ryangrowthh (bare article link, no text to judge), @mattyp botpfp (consumer side project) and the Grok-Bot-printer demo (fun, not a business).
research_notes:
Tool calls used: 11 of 12. Two Web Summary calls to fill in link-only posts: monid.ai (confirmed it is a 1,700+ tool gateway with a usage-based, not quality-based, leaderboard — which killed candidate 4, since the rankings surface is already taken and explicitly disclaims being a quality benchmark) and Tako/TakoViz (confirmed structured-data API, $7–$15 per 1,000 requests, which told me candidate 5's difficulty is licensing not engineering). I could not view any of the images or videos in the bookmarks, and the X article links (@ryangrowthh, @nateherk, @tsukiema_, @JayaGup10) had no titles or descriptions, so I judged those posts only on their visible text and set them aside rather than guessing.
Nine Web Search calls. Searches on FinOps/agent cost attribution returned a dense, mature field (Revenium, Mavvrik, nOps, PointFive, Zylo, TrueFoundry, FinOps Foundation token-economics WG) — that closed candidate 2. A search on formal verification surfaced the actual pstack docs in the Cursor plugins repo, confirming @poteto's work is an existing free plugin — that closed candidate 3. Searches on durable execution returned a crowded engine market (Temporal, Restate, Inngest, DBOS, Hatchet, Trigger.dev, Diagrid) but every source framed the guarantee as workflow-state persistence and crash recovery, with duplicate side effects listed as a *remaining* pitfall (Glean's "non-idempotent writes" note; "AI Agent Control Flow Patterns" listing double-executed side effects as a top-7 failure; the FINOS AI governance framework describing the crash-between-call-and-record window). Three further searches aimed specifically at finding a company selling reconciliation of agent write actions returned only research papers (an SSRN paper literally titled around duplicate side effects in LLM agents, an arXiv paper on evidence-guided recovery for ambiguous tool outcomes) and no commercial product. That absence is what raised Doublecheck's Gap score from a 6 to an 8 — with the caveat, stated in comparables, that absence of search evidence is weak evidence of absence.
prototype_summary: An operator console prototype where six ambiguous AI agent write-actions are reconciled into committed / not-committed / duplicated verdicts, surfacing an $89 double-charge, alongside blocked replays and a filterable effect ledger.
